article.title: How to Replace a Kitchen Faucet (Step by Step)
article.summary: Replace a kitchen faucet in an afternoon: shut off the water, free the old one with a basin wrench, mount the new faucet and test for leaks.
article.body:
Swapping a kitchen faucet is mostly a matter of reaching the nuts under the sink. This guide covers a standard top-mount faucet on a sink with working shut-off valves, including single-handle, two-handle and pull-down models.

Affiliate disclosure: some links in this guide are affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. We only recommend products we'd use ourselves.

Safety: wear safety glasses when you work under the sink, because grit and old corrosion fall into your eyes. If the sink has a garbage disposal, unplug it or switch off its breaker before you reach near it.

Steps

  1. Check the hole count and buy the right faucet

    Look under the sink and count the holes in the sink deck: one, two, three or four. A faucet with a deck plate can cover extra holes; a one-hole faucet can't fill a three-hole sink without one. Note whether you need a sprayer, soap dispenser or a pull-down spout that needs clearance under a window.

    Done right: the new faucet's box lists your hole count and it fits under any window or shelf above the sink.

  2. Shut off the water and relieve pressure

    Close both shut-off valves under the sink by turning them clockwise. Open the faucet to drain the lines. If a valve won't close fully or drips, close the main water valve instead and plan to replace that valve. Take a photo of all connections before you disconnect anything.

    Done right: with the faucet open, no water comes out.

  3. Disconnect and remove the old faucet

    Put a bucket under the valves and loosen the supply line nuts at the valves with an adjustable wrench. Unclip a pull-down hose's weight and quick-connect. Reach up behind the sink with a basin wrench to loosen the mounting nuts, then lift the faucet out from the top. Scrape old putty and grime off the sink deck and wipe it with rubbing alcohol.

    Done right: the sink deck is clean and dry, and the valves have only their bare outlets left.

  4. Mount the new faucet

    Follow the faucet's instructions for the seal: most use a rubber or plastic gasket under the base, some call for plumber's putty or silicone. Feed the lines through the hole, set the faucet straight, and have a helper hold it while you tighten the mounting nut or bracket from below. Snug it so the faucet can't twist, but don't crush the gasket.

    Done right: the faucet sits square to the back of the sink and doesn't rotate when you push the handle.

  5. Connect the water lines

    Connect hot to the left valve and cold to the right. Most new faucets have attached lines with 3/8 in compression ends; tighten each nut hand-tight plus a quarter to half turn with a wrench, holding the valve body steady with a second wrench. Compression fittings don't need thread tape. For a pull-down, click the hose into the quick-connect and clip on the weight at the mark shown in the instructions.

    Done right: no line is kinked, and the pull-down hose slides out and retracts smoothly.

  6. Flush, test and check for leaks

    Remove the aerator or spray head, open the valves slowly, and run water for a minute to flush out debris. Reinstall the aerator. Run hot and cold for a few minutes, then wipe each connection with a dry paper towel and check again an hour later.

    Done right: the paper towel stays dry at every joint and the spray pattern is even.

Call a plumber if: the shut-off valves are frozen or leaking, the supply pipes are corroded or soldered straight to the old faucet, or the sink is cracked around the faucet holes. A plumber can replace the valves in the same visit.

FAQ

How long does it take to replace a kitchen faucet?

About 1.5 to 3 hours for a first-timer. Most of the time goes into loosening old mounting nuts in a tight space.

Do I need a basin wrench?

Usually, yes. The mounting nuts sit behind the sink bowl where a normal wrench can't reach. A basin wrench costs about $15 to $25.

Can I install a single-hole faucet on a three-hole sink?

Yes, if the faucet comes with or accepts a deck plate (escutcheon) that covers the extra holes.

Should I replace the supply lines?

If the old lines are more than a few years old or are rigid copper, use new braided stainless lines. Many faucets now come with lines attached.
